lesson.title: Tangent Lines to Curves That Aren't Functions
lesson.summary: Once dy/dx is known at a point on an implicit curve, point-slope form gives the tangent line exactly as it would for any explicit function.
lesson.body:
Finding the equation of a tangent line to an implicit curve takes nothing new beyond what you already have: a point on the curve, the slope dy/dx at that point (found by implicit differentiation and solved for algebraically), and the point-slope form of a line, y - y_1 = m(x - x_1).

Go back to the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25 at the point (3, 4), where implicit differentiation gave dy/dx = -x/y = -3/4. Plug the point and the slope into point-slope form: y - 4 = -3/4 (x - 3). Distribute and simplify: y = -3/4 x + 9/4 + 4 = -3/4 x + 25/4. As a check, plug x = 3 back in: -3/4 (3) + 25/4 = -9/4 + 25/4 = 16/4 = 4, which matches the point, confirming the line is correct.

Circles offer a second, independent check that has nothing to do with calculus: a tangent line to a circle is always perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of tangency. The radius from the origin to (3, 4) has slope 4/3. The tangent line's slope is -3/4. Multiplying the two: (4/3)(-3/4) = -1, exactly the condition for perpendicular lines. Getting -1 here is strong evidence the derivative was computed correctly, and it is a good habit to look for a geometric check like this whenever the shape of the curve makes one available.

It is also worth noticing where the method breaks down. At the point (5, 0) on the same circle, dy/dx = -x/y = -5/0, which is undefined. That is not a mistake, it correctly signals a vertical tangent line, x = 5, at that point, something a formula written as y = f(x) could never represent directly but that implicit differentiation flags automatically through division by zero.
